The Jaliscan cotton rat (Sigmodon mascotensis) is a medium-sized rodent inhabiting the tropical deciduous forests and thornscrub of western Mexico. This oxygen consumption value, which reflects the energetic cost of maintaining homeostasis in a resting, post-absorptive state, is consistent with measurements reported for other members of the genus Sigmodon. The species exhibits a life history strategy characterized by moderately paced development relative to body size. Neonates, whose birth mass is estimated at 6.2 grams [Wwb = 6.2 grams] by extrapolation from the closely related hispid cotton rat (Sigmodon hispidus), are altricial at parturition, relying entirely on maternal care during the early postnatal period. This initial mass represents a modest fraction of the adult female body weight, setting the stage for a rapid growth phase that precedes independent foraging.

Females of Sigmodon mascotensis attain an ultimate adult body mass of 160 grams [Wwi = 160 grams], although field surveys report a range extending from 70 to 211 grams depending on habitat quality and seasonal resource availability. This variation in maximum wet weight likely reflects the influence of local precipitation patterns on the abundance of herbaceous food plants, which constitute the bulk of the diet. Under the stable thermal conditions typical of a controlled laboratory environment at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the gestation period spans approximately 27 days [tg = approximately 27 days], a duration that aligns closely with that of other sigmodontine rodents of comparable size. The relatively short gestation time suggests a trade-off between investment in prenatal development and the production of multiple litters within a single breeding season. Postnatal development proceeds through a series of well-defined milestones, beginning with the neonatal stage and culminating in nutritional independence from the dam.

The nursing pup transitions to solid food at weaning, which occurs 15 days after birth [tx = 15 days after birth] under captive conditions held at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This estimate, derived from data on Sigmodon hispidus, marks the cessation of lactation and the onset of independent feeding behavior. Weaning at this relatively early age permits the female to allocate resources toward subsequent reproductive efforts, a critical factor in a species that inhabits seasonally unpredictable environments. Following weaning, the juvenile enters a period of somatic growth and behavioral maturation before reaching reproductive competence. The progression from birth to this developmental landmark is governed by both intrinsic physiological mechanisms and extrinsic environmental cues, though the specific thresholds remain poorly documented for wild populations of this species. Field observations suggest that juvenile survival during the post-weaning phase is heavily influenced by predation risk and the availability of high-quality forage.

Sexual maturation in Sigmodon mascotensis is attained at 40 days after birth [tp = 40 days after birth] when individuals are reared at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a value extrapolated from the pattern observed in Sigmodon hispidus. This relatively rapid onset of puberty reflects the selective pressure to reproduce quickly in a seasonal habitat where favorable conditions may be transient. The adult lifespan, also based on records from Sigmodon hispidus, has been estimated at 5.2 years [am = 5.2 years] under laboratory conditions held at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], though mortality in natural populations is considerably higher due to predation and environmental stressors. This longevity, while modest compared to larger mammals, is notable among small rodents and permits multiple reproductive opportunities across consecutive breeding seasons. The interplay between early sexual maturity and extended lifespan suggests a life history strategy that balances the risks of juvenile mortality against the potential benefits of iteroparity.

Reproductive output in this species is characterized by small litters and a single annual breeding event. Females give birth to between 1 and 12 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 1 and 12 pups per litter], with a mean litter size that varies geographically and with maternal condition. Only one litter is produced each year [F_R_i = one litter is produced each year], a reproductive rate that is low relative to many other cricetid rodents of similar body mass. This constraint may reflect the energetic demands of lactation in a resource-limited environment, as the cost of provisioning a large litter would likely compromise maternal survival. The modest annual reproductive output is offset by the relatively long reproductive lifespan of adult females, which allows them to accumulate reproductive success over multiple years. Population dynamics are likely regulated by density-dependent factors such as food availability and territorial behavior, rather than by intrinsic reproductive potential alone.
